title: Solving Equations by Factorising
subject: Mathematics
subtopic: Common factor, difference of squares and trinomials

scenes.heading: Equations by Factorising
scenes.subheading: Grade 9 Mathematics · Factorisation and equations, part 3
scenes.narration: Welcome to part three of our Grade 9 series on factorisation and equations. In this lesson we solve equations by factorising, using every type of factorising we know.

scenes.heading: The method
bullets: Step 1: get zero on one side
Step 3: set each factor equal to zero
scenes.narration: If two factors multiply to give zero, then one of them must be zero. So here is the method. Step one: get zero on one side of the equation. Step two: factorise. Step three: set each factor equal to zero, and solve.

scenes.heading: Example 1: Common factor
scenes.narration: Solve x squared equals seven x. Get zero on one side: x squared minus seven x equals zero. Take out the common factor x: x times, x minus seven, equals zero. So x equals zero, or x equals seven.

scenes.heading: Example 2: Difference of squares
scenes.narration: Solve x squared minus twenty five equals zero. This is a difference of two squares: x minus five, times x plus five, equals zero. So x equals five, or x equals negative five.

scenes.heading: Example 3: Trinomial
scenes.narration: Solve x squared minus x equals six. Subtract six to get zero on one side: x squared minus x minus six equals zero. We need two numbers with product negative six and sum negative one: negative three and two. So x minus three, times x plus two, equals zero, and x equals three or x equals negative two.

scenes.heading: Example 4: Common factor first
scenes.narration: Solve two x squared, minus eight x, minus ten, equals zero. Take out the common factor two first. Then factorise the trinomial: negative five and one multiply to negative five and add to negative four. So two, times x minus five, times x plus one, equals zero. Two can never be zero, so x equals five, or x equals negative one.

scenes.heading: Example 5: Expand first
scenes.narration: Solve x times, x plus three, equals ten. Be careful: the right side is ten, not zero, so we cannot use the rule yet. Expand and subtract ten: x squared, plus three x, minus ten, equals zero. Five and negative two multiply to negative ten and add to three. So x equals negative five, or x equals two.

scenes.heading: Check your answers
scenes.narration: Let us check both answers in x times, x plus three, equals ten. When x is two: two times five is ten. When x is negative five: negative five times negative two is also ten. Both answers are correct.

scenes.heading: Tips
bullets: The rule only works when one side is zero
Never divide both sides by $x$: you lose $x = 0$
Take out a common factor first to make it easier
scenes.narration: Three tips. The rule only works when one side is zero, so always rearrange first. Never divide both sides by x, because you lose the answer x equals zero. And take out a common factor first, to make the trinomial easier.
